title: NCLAT: Group Companies Calling Themselves 'Hypothecators' Are Still Corporate Guarantors Under IBC
case_name: Bindu Kapoor v. Mamta Binani & Ors.
citation: NCLAT, order dated 6 November 2026, upholding NCLT Delhi's common order dated 7 April 2026
card_summary: The NCLAT dismissed four appeals by suspended director Bindu Kapoor and upheld insolvency against four Rana Kapoor-linked companies: Imagine Estate, Imagine Home, Imagine Residence and Imagine Habitat. It held the loan documents made them corporate guarantors of debt taken by Bliss House Private Limited, whatever label the documents used. All four cases stay before the NCLT Delhi bench under Section 60(2) of the IBC.
card_tip: A personal or group guarantee is tested by what the loan documents actually make the guarantor liable for, not by the term used for it on the signature page.
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: HNI (promoter family group facing personal and corporate guarantee exposure in insolvency). TARGET QUERY: can a company avoid being treated as a corporate guarantor under IBC by calling itself a hypothecator. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen (no search-volume or most-read data was seen; picked for being a fresh, well-reported appellate ruling on guarantor liability, a recurring HNI and family-business concern). Cross-verified across LiveLawBiz, Mondaq and CourtKutchehry, which agree on: NCLAT dismissed Bindu Kapoor's four appeals on 6 November 2026; the four appellant companies (named across sources as Imagine Estate, Imagine Home, Imagine Residence and Imagine Habitat Private Limited) were held liable as corporate guarantors of a loan taken by Bliss House Private Limited, part of the same Rana Kapoor-linked group; the NCLAT held Section 60(2) of the IBC keeps guarantor proceedings before the same bench as the principal corporate debtor's case, rejecting the argument that some appellant companies' Mumbai registered offices required a different forum; and the order upholds NCLT Delhi's common admission order of 7 April 2026. The exact loan amount is reported inconsistently across sources (figures from Rs 105 crore to aggregate figures in the hundreds of crores for the wider Rana Kapoor group of loans), so no specific amount is stated in this card. This is a civil insolvency finding on guarantor liability for admission purposes; it is not a finding of criminal wrongdoing against any individual, and a further appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.
